slides.0.title: Viticulture and climate: water, drought and sustainability
slides.0.subtitle: Dryland farming, the 2018 drought, IPW and BWI
slides.1.title: Water is the main constraint
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Winter rain, dry summers
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Rain falls in winter, so most vineyards are dryland or supplementally irrigated; inland areas (Robertson about 250–400 mm, Calitzdorp in the Klein Karoo about 200 mm, the Olifants River coastal plain about 150–200 mm) rely heavily on irrigation
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Water sources
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Robertson relies on the Breede River and dams such as Brandvlei and is comparatively water-secure in droughts; the Olifants River depends on the Clanwilliam Dam
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Earlier harvests
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Harvest dates have moved roughly two weeks earlier since the 1990s
slides.1.content: A frame often used in MW essays: climate (water) → viticulture (dryland, training) → quality and cost.
slides.2.title: The 2018 drought
slides.2.highlights.0.title: The forecast
slides.2.highlights.0.content: In January 2018 Vinpro and SAWIS expected the smallest wine grape crop since 2005; some estimates put the drop as high as 50% (a forecast, not a final figure)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Uneven impact
slides.2.highlights.1.content: The Olifants River was hit hardest, with producers allocated under 17% of their usual water quota (the Clanwilliam Dam was then about 19.9% full); the Orange River was the only region without shortages
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Day Zero
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Cape Town's 2018 water crisis (Day Zero) put water at the top of the whole industry's agenda, including water-saving irrigation and drought-tolerant varieties
slides.2.content: Drought hits yield and cost rather than simply quality; discuss them separately.
slides.3.title: Sustainability: IPW and BWI
slides.3.highlights.0.title: IPW
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Integrated Production of Wine, introduced in 1998, covers integrated pest management, reduced inputs and emissions, worker health and safety, biodiversity and wastewater, audited independently every three years
slides.3.highlights.1.title: The sustainability seal
slides.3.highlights.1.content: From the 2010 vintage producers whose vineyard, winery and bottling plant are all IPW accredited can carry the seal; the combined WO and IPW seal was on 88% of certified wines in 2024
slides.3.highlights.2.title: BWI
slides.3.highlights.2.content: The Biodiversity & Wine Initiative has promoted conservation in the Cape winelands since 2004; one source reports about 113,000 ha of conservation land on wine farms against about 101,000 ha of vineyard; IPW and BWI are separate schemes
slides.3.content: IPW is the industry-wide scheme; BWI focuses on biodiversity and conservation, and they can be joined independently.
